items.title: Anselm's ontological argument is a priori

options.text: An empirical argument from observation of nature
God is 'that than which no greater can be conceived'; existence in reality is greater than existence in the mind alone; therefore the greatest conceivable being must exist in reality
A historical argument from biblical events

items.reveal:
Anselm wrote the Proslogion (1077-78) as a contemplation aimed at finding 'a single argument' to prove God's existence. The famous formula appears in Proslogion 2.

Gaunilo (Anselm's contemporary) objected with his 'lost island' parody: by the same logic, the greatest conceivable island must exist. Anselm replied that the argument applies only to a necessary being, not contingent ones.

Descartes (Meditations V), Spinoza, Leibniz and Hegel reformulated versions. Kant's critique — existence is not a predicate (Critique of Pure Reason, 1781) — is the standard counter. Alvin Plantinga's modal version (1974) revived the argument using possible-world semantics.
items.why: The ontological argument is uniquely controversial. Almost everyone has the intuition that something is wrong with it — but the precise diagnosis (Gaunilo's? Kant's? Modal logic?) is itself contested philosophy.

items.title: Moral and natural evil are distinct problems
items.claim: What is the distinction between moral and natural evil?

options.text: All evil is caused by human moral failure

Moral evil is caused by free moral agents (murder, torture, cruelty); natural evil is caused by impersonal natural processes (earthquakes, disease, predation). They raise different problems for theism
Natural evil is just a subset of moral evil

items.reveal:
Free Will Defence (Augustine, Alvin Plantinga) explains moral evil as the cost of human free will — but doesn't obviously address natural evil. Earthquakes do not flow from human choices.

Irenaean theodicy (revived by John Hick, 'Evil and the God of Love', 1966) sees natural evil as part of soul-making — character development requires a challenging environment.

Augustinian theodicy treats evil as privatio boni (privation of good) — not a substance but an absence. The Fall extends moral consequences into nature.

The logical problem of evil (Mackie, 'Evil and Omnipotence', 1955) has been largely answered by Plantinga; the evidential problem (William Rowe, 1979) remains live.
items.why: The problem of evil is the most persistent challenge to classical theism. Its sub-distinctions (moral/natural, logical/evidential) shape which theodicies are even relevant — and a generic answer misses the structure of the argument.

items.title: Aquinas offered Five Ways, not one argument

options.text: Five distinct a posteriori arguments in Summa Theologiae I.2.3: motion (unmoved mover), causation (uncaused cause), contingency (necessary being), degree (greatest being), teleology (designer)

items.reveal:
Aquinas distinguishes a priori arguments (from concept to existence — Anselm's ontological) from a posteriori arguments (from observation). His Five Ways are all a posteriori — they begin from empirical features of the world.

First Way (motion): things move; an unmoved mover is required. Second Way (efficient causation): a first cause is required. Third Way (contingency): contingent things require a necessary being. Fourth Way (degree): degrees of perfection require a maximum. Fifth Way (teleology): purposive ordering requires a designer.

Each has been criticised separately. Hume and Kant attacked the cosmological framework; Darwinian biology challenges the teleological reading; Russell's exchange with Copleston (1948 BBC debate) challenged the contingency argument.
items.why: Aquinas is sometimes reduced to a single 'cosmological argument'. He offered five distinct arguments that need to be evaluated separately — and Catholic natural theology still rests on this framework.
